newsitem.title: USA: Emerging debt takes breather, high yielders firm.
newsitem.headline: Emerging debt takes breather, high yielders firm.

text.p: Emerging market debts were mixed Monday, in a consolidating mode after last week's rally.
Most assests outperformed the U.S. Treasuries, with high yielders like Bulgaria and Ecuador holding better than the major Latin Bradys, traders said.
"Last week's flow was incredible," said a trader, referring to the fresh funds invested in emerging market assets. "People are looking for yields."
Bulgaria FLRB rose 1.00 to 53-1/4 bid and Ecuador PDI added 3/8 to 66-1/8 bid.
Bull runs on Russia Vnesh loan participations took a pause, but the underlying sentiment was upbeat.
Russia Vnesh made a new high at 90.00 before slipping to 89-1/2 bid, unchanged on the day.
Over the weekend, a senior Russian official said the government would set the date for signing a rescheduling agreement with London club of commerical bank creditors in July.

"They have a powerful incentive to conclude the deal," said Peter Allen, head of emerging market research at BankBoston Securities, noting that at least new issuance totalling $2.5 billion this year in addition to the 10-year global bond whose roadshow was set to begin on Wednesday.
In 1998, $9.8 billion issuance was planned, he said.
Gretchen Rodkey, East European and Russian debt analyst at Bear Stearns, said the July target for signing the definitive terms of the restructuring agreement was "reasonable but ambitious."
Russian officials said 80 percent of the debt was reconciled and they needed 90 percent before the agreement.

Given the complexity of reconciliation, some delay could not ruled out, but Rodkey expected the the deal, which takes place six weeks after the definitive terms are reached, to close before the end of the year.

Venezuela Brady bonds, which enjoyed a sharp run-up last week on its sovereign credit rating upgrade, extended the gains. S&P last Thursday lifted Venezuela's long-term foreign currency debt rating to single B plus from single B.
Venezuela DCB at 93.00 and Venezuela FLIRB at 93-3/8 were making new highs. They were bid 92-3/4, up 1/2 and 92-7/8, up 7/8, in afternoon trading.
Allen said that the allure of Venezuela at the moment was the prospect of a Brady bond buyback.
"Venezuela is riding on the coattail of Brazil as the next candidate for exchange," he said. Brazil issued a $3 billion 30-year global bond last week.
The successful oil field sales also whet investors' appetites for Venezula risk, Allen siad.
S&P's credit action, by comparison, was less important because the upgrade was overdue and the one-notch rise fell short of some investors' expectations, he added.

To take a bullish stance on Venezuela, Allen favored Par bonds and discount bonds for their longer duration and relative value to DCB and FLIRB. Venezuela Par rose 3/8 to 78-3/4 and Discount climbed 5/8 to 88-1/4 bid.
